questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's FAQs on accounts of non-residents, interest earned in which of the following rupee accounts is exempt from income tax?

options.text: Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) account
Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) account
Special Non-Resident Rupee (SNRR) account
Resident savings account of a returning NRI

solution.explanation: RBI's comparison table states that income earned in NRE accounts is exempt from income tax (and the balances from wealth tax), whereas income in NRO accounts is taxable.
solution.why_others_wrong: NRO income is taxable; SNRR is a non-interest bearing business account; a resident account earns taxable interest.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) account

questions.question_text: Under RBI's KYC rules, a demand draft, pay order or traveller's cheque can be purchased against cash only if its amount is:

options.text: Less than ₹10,000
Less than ₹20,000
Less than ₹50,000

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Master Direction – Deposits and Accounts (FEMA), which of the following is NOT permitted in respect of balances held in an Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency (EEFC) account?

options.text: Crediting the balances to NRE/FCNR(B) accounts when the holder becomes a non-resident
Obtaining fund-based or non-fund-based credit facilities against the balances
Repaying packing credit advances to the extent exports have actually taken place
Making payments outside India for permitted current or capital account transactions

solution.explanation: The Master Direction lists the features of the EEFC scheme: it is a non-interest bearing account; balances may be used for permitted payments abroad, to repay packing credit to the extent exports have taken place, and may be credited to NRE/FCNR(B) accounts on a change of residential status. Fund-based or non-fund-based credit facilities should not be granted against EEFC balances.
steps: Permitted: payments abroad, packing credit repayment, transfer to NRE/FCNR(B) on becoming NR
Not permitted: credit facilities against EEFC balances
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three uses are expressly allowed by the Master Direction.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Obtaining fund-based or non-fund-based credit facilities against the balances

fact_checks.claim: Fund-based/ non-fund based credit facilities should not be granted against the balances held in EEFC Accounts; Exporters can repay packing credit advances ... from balances in their EEFC account to the extent exports have actually taken place; Balances held in the account may be credited to NRE/ FCNR (B) Accounts ... consequent upon change of their residential status; Debits: Payment outside India towards capital or current account transactions

questions.question_text: Under the definition used in RBI's FAQs on accounts of non-residents, a 'Person of Indian Origin' (PIO) is a person resident outside India who is a citizen of any country other than:

options.text: Bangladesh or Pakistan, or any other country specified by the Central Government
Nepal or Bhutan, or any other country specified by RBI
China or Afghanistan only
Sri Lanka or Myanmar only

solution.explanation: A PIO is a person resident outside India who is a citizen of any country other than Bangladesh or Pakistan (or another country specified by the Central Government) and meets conditions such as having been an Indian citizen, or being the child, grandchild or great-grandchild or foreign-origin spouse of such a person. OCI cardholders resident outside India are included.
steps: PIO excludes citizens of Bangladesh and Pakistan
solution.why_others_wrong: Nepal/Bhutan, China/Afghanistan and Sri Lanka/Myanmar are not the excluded countries named.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Bangladesh or Pakistan, or any other country specified by the Central Government

Seven days to ten years, as for resident term deposits
One to three years, though banks may accept longer deposits from their asset-liability point of view
Only for exactly one year, renewable annually

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Three foreign nationals of non-Indian origin visiting India opened NRO savings accounts with money remitted from abroad. A held his account for 5 months and it received only remittances from abroad and interest. B held hers for 8 months with only remittances and interest. C held his for 4 months, but it was also credited with ₹20,000 of local fees. Who can have the balance paid out to them at the time of departure under RBI's rules?

options.text: A and B only
A and C only
A only
A, B and C

solution.explanation: A tourist's NRO balance may be paid at departure provided the account was maintained for not more than six months and was not credited with any local funds other than interest. A meets both conditions; B exceeds six months; C received local funds.
steps: Condition 2: no local credits except interest → A, B
solution.why_others_wrong: B fails the six-month condition; C fails the no-local-funds condition.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: An exporter receives USD 50,000 of export proceeds in its EEFC account in March 2026 and, in April, uses USD 20,000 of these March accruals for an approved import payment; it has no forward commitments. Under RBI's Master Direction – Deposits and Accounts, how much of the March accruals must be converted into rupees, and by when?

options.text: USD 50,000, on or before 31 March 2026
USD 30,000, on or before 31 March 2027
Nothing, because EEFC balances never need conversion
USD 30,000, on or before 30 April 2026

solution.explanation: 100% of foreign exchange earnings can be credited to EEFC, but the total accruals of a calendar month must be converted into rupees on or before the last day of the succeeding calendar month, after adjusting for use for approved purposes or forward commitments. March accruals of 50,000 less 20,000 used leaves USD 30,000 to convert by 30 April 2026.
steps: Deadline: last day of the next month = 30 April 2026
solution.why_others_wrong: Conversion is net of approved use and due by the end of the following month, not the same month or a year later; balances are not exempt from conversion.
solution.final_answer: Option D: USD 30,000, on or before 30 April 2026

fact_checks.claim: Credits permitted: 100 percent of the foreign exchange earnings by way of inward remittance ...; the sum total of the accruals in the account during a calendar month should be converted into Rupees on or before the last day of the succeeding calendar month after adjusting for utilization of the balances for approved purposes or forward commitments

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Priya lives in Chennai, but the OVD she has shows her old New Delhi address. To open an account in Chennai she can offer: (P) an electricity bill dated six weeks ago, (Q) a post-paid mobile bill dated three months ago, (R) a municipal property tax receipt. Under RBI's KYC Directions, 2025 for commercial banks, which can serve as deemed OVDs for proof of address, and what must she do afterwards?

options.text: P, Q and R; no further document is needed
P and R; submit an OVD with her current address within three months
R only; submit an OVD with her current address within one year
P and Q; submit an OVD with her current address within 30 days

solution.explanation: If the OVD does not show the current address, a customer may give a deemed OVD such as a utility bill not more than two months old or a property/municipal tax receipt, but must submit an OVD with the current address within three months. The three-month-old mobile bill is too old.
steps: Utility bill ≤ 2 months → P valid, Q not
OVD with current address within 3 months
solution.why_others_wrong: Q is older than two months; the follow-up OVD is due within three months, not one year or 30 days, and it is required.
solution.final_answer: Option B: P and R; submit an OVD with her current address within three months

fact_checks.claim: when the customer furnishes an OVD that does not have an updated address, the bank shall deem ... utility bill which is not more than two months old of any service provider (electricity, telephone, post-paid mobile phone ...); property or Municipal tax receipt ... the customer shall submit OVD with current address within a period of three months of submitting the documents specified at (b) above

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Rahul, an NRI, holds an NRE savings account and a three-year FCNR(B) deposit. He returns to India to take up employment. According to RBI's FAQs, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Both accounts must be closed on his return and the money credited to a resident savings account
The NRE account may continue as an NRE account until he has stayed in India for 182 days
The NRE account must at once be redesignated as a resident account or moved to an RFC account, while the FCNR(B) deposit may continue till maturity at the contracted rate
The FCNR(B) deposit must be broken immediately, while the NRE account can continue till he chooses to close it

solution.explanation: On return for employment, NRE accounts should be designated as resident accounts, or the funds transferred to RFC accounts at the holder's option, immediately. FCNR(B) deposits may continue till maturity at the contracted rate; on maturity they are converted into resident rupee or RFC accounts.
steps: NRE → redesignate as resident / transfer to RFC immediately
solution.why_others_wrong: Closure is not required, the NRE status does not wait 182 days, and FCNR(B) need not be broken.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The NRE account must at once be redesignated as a resident account or moved to an RFC account, while the FCNR(B) deposit may continue till maturity at the contracted rate

fact_checks.claim: NRE accounts should be designated as resident accounts or the funds held in these accounts may be transferred to the RFC accounts, at the option of the account holder, immediately upon the return of the account holder to India for taking up employment ... FCNR (B) deposits may be allowed to continue till maturity at the contracted rate of interest

questions.question_text: Consider the following statements: I. The amalgamation of Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India into Punjab National Bank was a scheme framed by RBI under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act. II. The amalgamation of The Lakshmi Vilas Bank with DBS Bank India Ltd. came into force on 27 November 2020, from when LVB's branches functioned as DBS Bank India branches. III. Both these amalgamations were sanctioned under section 9 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts. Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
II only

solution.explanation: The OBC/UBI scheme was issued by the Government of India under section 9 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts of 1970 and 1980, not by RBI. LVB, a private sector lender under moratorium, was amalgamated with DBS Bank India through a scheme that RBI itself drafted and placed in the public domain for objections; it took effect on 27 November 2020. Being a private bank, LVB was outside the bank nationalisation Acts.

III: false (LVB was not a nationalised bank)
solution.why_others_wrong: Statements I and III are wrong, so every option containing them is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: II only

solution.final_answer: Option D: T-bill 113 bps, CP 70 bps, CD 43 bps – all now below the 125 bps repo cut

fact_checks.claim: the WACR, the 3-month T-bill rate, the 3-month CP issued by NBFCs, and the 3-month CD rate declined by 89 bps, 119 bps, 143 bps, and 127 bps, respectively up to end-December, 2025. However, since the beginning of January and up to February 4, 2026, the 3-month T-bill rate, the 3-month CP issued by NBFCs, and the 3-month CD rate have hardened by 6 bps, 73 bps and 84 bps, respectively

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's amendment directions of 7 October 2026 revise the methodology for minimum capital requirements for counterparty credit risk from 1 April 2027. To which commercial banks do they apply mandatorily?

options.text: Banks with an international presence or with derivatives outstanding (book value) of ₹25,000 crore and above
Only the Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs)
All commercial banks, including small finance banks and payments banks
Only foreign banks operating in India through branches

solution.concept: Scope of the revised counterparty credit risk framework
solution.explanation: The Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions Amendment Directions, 2026 (7 October 2026), effective 1 April 2027, apply to commercial banks with an international presence or with book value of derivatives outstanding of ₹25,000 crore and above on a consolidated group-wide basis. The remaining commercial banks may choose either the Current Exposure Method (CEM) or the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR).
steps: Mandatory: international presence, or derivatives book ≥ ₹25,000 crore
solution.why_others_wrong: The scope is not defined by D-SIB status or by foreign ownership, and other banks are given a choice rather than being covered mandatorily.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Banks with an international presence or with derivatives outstanding (book value) of ₹25,000 crore and above

fact_checks.claim: These Amendment Directions shall come into effect from April 1, 2027; shall be applicable to commercial banks with an international presence or with book value of derivative outstanding of ₹ 25,000 crore and above as on the reporting date, on a consolidated group wide basis. However, remaining commercial banks may choose to adopt either the Current Exposure Method (CEM) or the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's circular of 23 September 2026 notified a Government of India-supported Line of Credit extended by Exim Bank to which country, for ₹4,850 crore?

options.text: Sri Lanka
Maldives
Mauritius
Bangladesh

solution.final_answer: Option B: Maldives

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: By a circular of 1 October 2026 on online submission of Form A2 for outward remittances, what did RBI change for Authorised Dealers' internal guidelines?

options.text: They must now be approved by RBI before use
They can be framed only for remittances up to USD 25,000 a year
They may be approved by the Board or by a Board Committee/Management Committee to which the Board has delegated powers
They now need approval of the Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India

The October 2026 circular allows approval by the Board or any Board Committee or Management Committee with delegated powers; other instructions remain unchanged.
solution.why_others_wrong: No RBI pre-approval or FEDAI approval is required; the circular adds no amount ceiling.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They may be approved by the Board or by a Board Committee/Management Committee to which the Board has delegated powers

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's amendment of 22 September 2026 to the commercial banks' investment portfolio directions, how must a bank value units of an unlisted InvIT or REIT that fails to compute and disclose its NAV as required by SEBI?

options.text: At face value
At ₹1 per unit
At the last traded price on any exchange
At cost less 50%

solution.explanation: Unquoted InvIT and REIT units are valued at the NAV the trust discloses. If the trust fails to compute and disclose NAV in the manner and frequency SEBI specifies, or the units are infrequently traded, they are valued at ₹1 – a conservative rule.
solution.why_others_wrong: Face value, last traded price and cost-based haircuts are not the prescribed treatment.
solution.final_answer: Option B: At ₹1 per unit

fact_checks.claim: Units: The valuation shall be done at the NAV as disclosed by the InvIT. Where an InvIT fails to compute and disclose the NAV in the manner and frequency specified under SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, the value of its units shall be treated as ₹1

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
RBI's amendment directions of 1 October 2026 on acquisition of shares in banks introduced a one-time approval for 'qualifying persons'. Consider:
I. Qualifying persons are SEBI-registered mutual funds, PFRDA-registered pension funds and IRDAI-registered insurers that do not belong to the bank's promoter group or group.
II. The one-time approval covers subsequent acquisitions of major shareholding up to 10% of the bank's paid-up capital or voting rights, on an aggregate basis.
III. With the one-time approval, prior approval is no longer needed even for the initial acquisition of major shareholding.
Which is/are correct?

options.text: II only
II and III only
I, II and III
I and II only

solution.explanation: I and II follow the amendment's definitions and proviso. III is wrong: RBI said prior approval stays mandatory for the initial acquisition of major shareholding; the relief is only for subsequent acquisitions after a holding has fallen below 5%. Applications go through PRAVAAH.
steps: III: initial acquisition still needs prior approval
solution.why_others_wrong: 'II only' omits I; options with III are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and II only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's income recognition and asset classification norms, advances against certain instruments need not be treated as NPAs if adequate margin is available. Advances against which of the following are NOT covered by this exemption?

options.text: Gold ornaments
Term deposits
Kisan Vikas Patras
Life insurance policies

solution.explanation: RBI's IRAC Directions, 2025 exempt advances against term deposits, NSCs eligible for surrender, KVPs and life insurance policies from NPA treatment as long as adequate margin is available. Advances against gold ornaments, government securities and all other securities are expressly not covered.
steps: Exempt (with adequate margin): term deposits, NSCs, KVPs, life insurance policies
Not exempt: gold ornaments, government securities, other securities
solution.why_others_wrong: Term deposits, KVPs and life insurance policies are all in the exempted list.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Gold ornaments

fact_checks.claim: Advances against term deposits, NSCs eligible for surrender, KVPs and life insurance policies need not be treated as NPAs, provided adequate margin is available; advances against gold ornaments, government securities and all other securities are not covered by this exemption

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), the regulator that implements the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, was established on:

options.text: 1 December 2016
1 October 2016
1 April 2017

solution.explanation: IBBI was established on 1 October 2016 under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. It is a key pillar of the ecosystem that implements the Code (it marks 1 October as its Annual Day).
steps: IBBI established under the Code on 1 October 2016
solution.why_others_wrong: The other dates are not IBBI's establishment date.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1 October 2016

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Asset reconstruction companies (ARCs) registered under the SARFAESI Act acquire stressed loans and issue security receipts (SRs). According to RBI's FAQs on ARCs, what is the maximum realisation period for financial assets acquired by an ARC?

options.text: Three years from the date of acquisition
Five years from the date of acquisition
Ten years from the date of acquisition
Eight years from the date of acquisition

solution.explanation: RBI's ARC FAQs (September 2026) refer to the maximum realisation period of 8 years from the date of acquisition. A transferee ARC cannot issue SRs to other qualified buyers for such assets after the eight-year period from the first acquisition has expired.
steps: ARC acquires asset and issues SRs
solution.why_others_wrong: Three, five and ten years are not the prescribed window.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Eight years from the date of acquisition

fact_checks.claim: ARCs are not prohibited from transferring financial assets to another ARC even after completion of the maximum realisation period of 8 years from the date of acquisition, but the transferee ARC shall not issue SRs to other QBs after the expiry of the stipulated eight-year period

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank's loan is backed by a guarantee of the Central Government. Interest has been overdue for more than 90 days. Under RBI's IRAC Directions, 2025, when will this account be treated as an NPA?

options.text: Only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked
Immediately, since interest is overdue for more than 90 days
Only after it remains overdue for 12 months
Never, since sovereign-guaranteed loans are always standard

solution.explanation: Credit facilities backed by a Central Government guarantee, though overdue, are treated as NPA only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked. This exemption is not for income recognition. State Government guaranteed advances, by contrast, follow the normal 90-day norm.
steps: Central Government guarantee → NPA only on repudiation when invoked
State Government guarantee → normal 90-day overdue norm
solution.why_others_wrong: The 90-day norm applies to State (not Central) Government guaranteed advances; there is no 12-month rule; the account is not standard for ever, as repudiation makes it an NPA.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked

fact_checks.claim: The credit facilities backed by guarantee of the Central Government though overdue shall be treated as NPA only when the Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked; State Government guaranteed advances attract the norms if dues remain overdue for more than 90 days

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: When a fraud is detected in a borrower account, a bank must normally provide for the entire amount due immediately. To smooth the impact on quarterly profits, over what maximum period may it spread this provision?

options.text: Two quarters after the fraud is reported
Four quarters, starting with the quarter in which the fraud is detected
Eight quarters from the date of the fraud
Until the end of the next financial year

solution.explanation: Under the IRAC Directions, a bank has the option to make the fraud provision over a period not exceeding four quarters, commencing with the quarter of detection. If this spills into the next financial year, the unprovided amount at year-end is debited to 'other reserves'.
steps: Option: spread over up to four quarters from the quarter of detection
solution.why_others_wrong: Two quarters is too short; eight quarters and 'end of next year' exceed the four-quarter limit.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Four quarters, starting with the quarter in which the fraud is detected

fact_checks.claim: A bank shall normally provide for the entire amount due immediately upon a fraud being detected; it has the option to make the provisions over a period not exceeding four quarters, commencing from the quarter in which the fraud has been detected

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: What provision must a bank hold on its standard-account exposure to a company that has a director (other than a nominee director of a government or financial institution brought in at the time of distress) whose name appears more than once in the list of wilful defaulters?

options.text: 0.40 per cent
1 per cent
5 per cent
15 per cent

solution.explanation: The IRAC Directions prescribe a provision of 5% on existing loans or exposures to companies with such director(s), even when the accounts are standard, well above the normal standard-asset rate.
steps: Director appears more than once in wilful defaulter list
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.40% is the general standard-asset rate; 1% applies to commercial real estate; 15% is the substandard rate.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 5 per cent

fact_checks.claim: The provisioning in respect of existing loans / exposures to companies having director(s) (other than nominee directors of government / financial institutions brought on board at the time of distress), whose name(s) appear more than once in the list of wilful defaulters, shall be five per cent in cases of standard accounts

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's FAQs on asset reconstruction companies (September 2026), can an ARC restructure a borrower account that the lender has classified as fraud or wilful defaulter?

options.text: Yes, if the restructuring is approved by the ARC's Board
No, unless the existing promoters are replaced and the company is totally delinked from them
Yes, but only by converting debt into equity
No, and the ARC must sell such accounts within one year

solution.explanation: ARCs are not permitted to restructure accounts classified as fraud or wilful defaulter. Restructuring includes rescheduling, conversion of debt into equity and additional funding. The exception: where the existing promoters are replaced by new promoters and the borrower company is totally delinked from the erstwhile promoters/management, the ARC may consider restructuring based on viability.
steps: Fraud / wilful defaulter accounts → no restructuring by ARC
Exception: promoters replaced and company delinked from them
solution.why_others_wrong: Board approval does not override the bar; debt-equity conversion is itself a form of restructuring; there is no one-year sale rule.
solution.final_answer: Option B: No, unless the existing promoters are replaced and the company is totally delinked from them

fact_checks.claim: ARCs are not permitted to restructure borrower accounts classified as fraud/ wilful defaulter; however, where the existing promoters are replaced by new promoters and the borrower company is totally delinked from such erstwhile promoters/management, ARCs may take a view on restructuring based on viability

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Under RBI's IRAC Directions, 2025, certain agricultural loans follow the crop-season norms for NPA classification instead of the 90-day norm. Which of the following loans qualify for the crop-season norms?
P. ₹50 lakh to an individual farmer against pledge of his produce for 10 months
Q. ₹75 lakh to an individual farmer against pledge of his produce for 6 months
R. ₹2 crore to a farmer producer organisation (aggregate borrowing ₹3 crore) against pledge of produce for 9 months
S. ₹2 crore to a corporate farmer against pledge of produce for 15 months

options.text: P, Q and R only
P only
R and S only
P and R only

solution.concept: Agricultural loans and crop-season NPA norms
solution.explanation: Crop-season norms apply to pledge loans to individual farmers up to ₹60 lakh for not more than 12 months, and to corporate farmers, FPOs, partnership firms and co-operatives of farmers (aggregate limit ₹4 crore per borrower) for pledge loans up to ₹2.5 crore for not more than 12 months. Other agricultural loans follow the 90-day norm.
steps: R: aggregate ₹3 crore ≤ ₹4 crore; ₹2 crore ≤ ₹2.5 crore; 9 months → qualifies
solution.why_others_wrong: Q exceeds the ₹60 lakh cap for individuals; S exceeds the 12-month period.
solution.final_answer: Option D: P and R only

fact_checks.claim: Crop-season norms apply to loans to individual farmers up to ₹60 lakh against pledge / hypothecation of agricultural produce for a period not exceeding twelve months, and to loans to corporate farmers, FPOs, partnership firms and co-operatives of farmers up to an aggregate limit of ₹4 crore per borrower, including loans up to ₹2.5 crore against pledge of produce for not more than twelve months; other agricultural loans follow the 90 days delinquency norm

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The first paper issued by the Basel Committee, in 1975, came to be known as the 'Concordat'. What did it deal with?

options.text: Sharing supervisory responsibility for banks' foreign establishments between host and home supervisors
A minimum capital ratio of 8% of risk-weighted assets
Capital requirements for market risk using internal models
Liquidity standards to survive a 30-day stress period

solution.explanation: The 1975 Concordat set out principles for sharing supervisory responsibility for banks' foreign branches, subsidiaries and joint ventures between host and parent (home) supervisors, to close gaps in international supervisory coverage. It was revised in May 1983.
steps: 1975 Concordat → home/host supervision of foreign establishments
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options describe later Basel standards.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Sharing supervisory responsibility for banks' foreign establishments between host and home supervisors

fact_checks.claim: The 1975 paper known as the Concordat set out principles for sharing supervisory responsibility for banks' foreign branches, subsidiaries and joint ventures between host and parent (or home) supervisory authorities

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Basel Committee's 'Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision', first published in September 1997 with 25 principles, now contain how many principles after the latest revision in April 2024?

solution.explanation: The Core Principles began with 25 basic principles in 1997. After several revisions, most recently in April 2024, the document now includes 29 principles.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 was the original number; 24 (the CPMI-IOSCO PFMIs) and 30 are distractors.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 29

fact_checks.claim: When first published in September 1997, the paper set out 25 basic principles; after several revisions, most recently in April 2024, the document now includes 29 principles

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Basel III introduced two liquidity standards. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio covers funding needs over a 30-day stress period. What is the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) intended to address?

options.text: Intraday liquidity needs in payment systems
Maturity mismatches over the entire balance sheet
Concentration of large exposures to one counterparty
Losses from operational failures

solution.explanation: In the Basel Committee's description, the LCR is meant to provide enough cash for a 30-day stress period, while the NSFR is a longer-term ratio intended to address maturity mismatches over the entire balance sheet.
steps: NSFR: longer term, maturity mismatch across the balance sheet
solution.why_others_wrong: Intraday liquidity, large exposures and operational risk are covered by other standards.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Maturity mismatches over the entire balance sheet

fact_checks.claim: Basel III liquidity requirements: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), intended to provide enough cash to cover funding needs over a 30-day period of stress; and a longer-term ratio, the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), intended to address maturity mismatches over the entire balance sheet

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which Basel III requirement sets a minimum amount of loss-absorbing capital relative to all of a bank's assets and off-balance sheet exposures, regardless of risk weighting?

options.text: Leverage ratio
Capital conservation buffer
Countercyclical capital buffer
Liquidity Coverage Ratio

solution.concept: Leverage ratio as a non-risk-based measure
solution.explanation: The Basel III leverage ratio is a simple, non-risk-based backstop: capital relative to total exposures, irrespective of risk weights. The buffers are add-ons to risk-based capital, and the LCR is a liquidity measure.
solution.why_others_wrong: The two buffers are percentages of risk-weighted assets; the LCR concerns liquid assets, not capital.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Leverage ratio

fact_checks.claim: Basel III includes a leverage ratio - a minimum amount of loss-absorbing capital relative to all of a bank's assets and off-balance sheet exposures regardless of risk weighting

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Basel Committee completed its Basel III post-crisis reforms in 2017. Which element of these reforms limits the extent to which banks can use internal models to reduce their risk-based capital requirements?

options.text: The capital conservation buffer
The Pillar 3 disclosure framework
The output floor, based on the revised standardised approaches
The Net Stable Funding Ratio

solution.explanation: The 2017 reforms revised the standardised approaches for credit, CVA and operational risk and added a revised leverage ratio, a leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs and an output floor. The output floor is based on the revised standardised approaches and limits how far internal models can reduce RWAs, to cut excessive variability in risk-weighted assets.
steps: Purpose: curb RWA variability from internal models
solution.why_others_wrong: The conservation buffer restricts payouts; Pillar 3 is disclosure; the NSFR is a funding ratio.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The output floor, based on the revised standardised approaches

fact_checks.claim: The final reforms also include a revised leverage ratio, a leverage ratio buffer for global systemically important banks and an output floor, based on the revised standardised approaches, which limits the extent to which banks can use internal models to reduce risk-based capital requirements

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer's non-callable fixed deposit, normally excluded from a bank's LCR computation, is pledged as collateral for a loan to the customer. Under RBI's LCR amendments effective 1 April 2026, how is this deposit treated?

options.text: It stays excluded, as it is contractually non-callable
As Level 1 high-quality liquid assets of the bank
As a deduction from the bank's CET1 capital
As a callable deposit for LCR purposes

solution.explanation: RBI's April 2025 circular (effective 1 April 2026) says that a deposit hitherto excluded from LCR computation, such as a non-callable FD, that is contractually pledged as collateral for a credit facility shall be treated as callable for LCR purposes, so it attracts the relevant run-off.
steps: Pledged against a loan → treated as callable for LCR
solution.why_others_wrong: It does not stay excluded; a customer deposit is a liability, not the bank's HQLA; it has nothing to do with CET1 deductions.
solution.final_answer: Option D: As a callable deposit for LCR purposes

fact_checks.claim: In case a deposit, hitherto excluded from LCR computation (for instance, a non-callable fixed deposit), is contractually pledged as collateral to secure a credit facility or loan, such deposit shall be treated as callable for LCR purposes; these amendments come into force from April 01, 2026

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank has HQLA of ₹1,350 crore and total net cash outflows of ₹1,500 crore over the next 30 days, computed under the earlier rules. These outflows include ₹400 crore of deposits from educational trusts and partnership firms (not small business customers), which ran off at 100%. Under RBI's LCR amendments effective 1 April 2026, such funding is treated as from non-financial corporates. Assuming nothing else changes, how does the bank's LCR move?

options.text: From 90% to 100%, just meeting the minimum
From 90% to about 95.1%, still below the minimum
From 90% to about 107.1%, crossing the 100% minimum
It stays at 90%, as only retail deposits were affected

solution.concept: LCR = HQLA ÷ total net cash outflows over 30 days
solution.explanation: Funding from trusts, AoPs, partnerships, LLPs etc. (not treated as SBCs) now attracts a 40% run-off instead of 100%. Outflow on ₹400 crore falls from ₹400 crore to ₹160 crore, so net outflows fall to ₹1,260 crore.
steps: New outflow on trust deposits = 40% × 400 = ₹160 crore
solution.why_others_wrong: 100% ignores the reduced outflow's full effect; 95.1% would apply a smaller cut; the change applies to trusts and partnerships, not only retail deposits.
solution.final_answer: Option C: From 90% to about 107.1%, crossing the 100% minimum

fact_checks.claim: Funding from non-financial entities such as trusts (educational/religious/charitable), AoPs, partnerships, proprietorships, LLPs and other incorporated entities shall be categorised as funding from 'non-financial corporates' and attract a run-off rate of 40 per cent (as against 100 per cent currently prescribed), unless treated as SBCs; effective April 01, 2026

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the evolution of the Basel framework, as described by the Basel Committee:
I. The 1988 Accord's minimum capital ratio was to be implemented by the end of 1992.
II. The Market Risk Amendment of 1996 introduced the leverage ratio for the first time.
III. Basel III added a capital conservation buffer that, when breached, restricts payouts, with most reforms phased in between 2013 and 2019.
Which of the above is/are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III

solution.explanation: The 1988 Accord called for an 8% minimum to be implemented by end-1992 (I correct). The 1996 amendment added capital for market risk and allowed internal VaR models; the leverage ratio came only with Basel III (II wrong). Basel III added the capital conservation buffer, which restricts payouts when breached, with most reforms phased in between 2013 and 2019 (III correct).
steps: II ✗ (leverage ratio is a Basel III element)
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option including II is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The 1988 Accord called for a minimum ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets of 8% to be implemented by the end of 1992

The Market Risk Amendment (January 1996) incorporated a capital requirement for market risks; Basel III adds a capital conservation buffer that, when breached, restricts payouts, and a leverage ratio; most of the reforms are being phased in between 2013 and 2019

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: When a bank trades Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) on RBI's e-Kuber portal, how is the counterparty decided?

options.text: Orders are matched anonymously by the portal; the bank cannot select the counterparty
The buying bank selects the seller from a list of offers
NABARD allots a seller to each buyer
Buyer and seller negotiate bilaterally and report the deal to RBI

solution.explanation: RBI's PSL FAQs state that order matching on the e-Kuber PSLC module is anonymous; neither buyer nor seller can select the counterparty. Partial matching can happen depending on premium and lots available. No transaction fee is charged for using the module.
steps: Anonymous order matching; no counterparty selection
solution.why_others_wrong: Buyers cannot pick sellers; NABARD has no allotment role; PSLCs are not bilateral OTC deals.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Orders are matched anonymously by the portal; the bank cannot select the counterparty

fact_checks.claim: The order matching will be done on anonymous basis through the portal and the buyer/seller cannot select the counterparty; partial matching will happen depending on the matching of premium and availability of category-wise PSLC lots

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Bank X sold a PSLC to Bank Y. Later, an RBI inspection finds that the loans underlying the PSLC were not eligible for priority sector classification. According to RBI's FAQs, whose achievement is reduced?

options.text: Only the buyer's (Bank Y), as it used the certificate
Both banks' equally
Neither bank's, since the PSLC has expired on 31 March
Only the seller's (Bank X); the buyer bears no risk

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say misclassifications, if any, are reduced from the achievement of the PSLC seller bank only. There is no risk for the PSLC buyer even if the underlying asset is later found ineligible.
steps: PSLC sold by X, bought by Y
Underlying declassified → X's achievement reduced; Y unaffected
solution.why_others_wrong: The buyer is protected; the loss is not shared; expiry does not erase the seller's misclassification.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Only the seller's (Bank X); the buyer bears no risk

fact_checks.claim: The misclassifications, if any, will have to be reduced from the achievement of PSLC seller bank only. There will be no risk for the PSLC buyer, even if the underlying asset of the traded PSLC gets misclassified

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank that missed its priority sector targets has outstanding shortfall deposits with NABARD, SIDBI and NHB. According to RBI's PSL FAQs, how are these deposits treated?

options.text: They count only towards the overall PSL target, not any sub-target, and are excluded from ANBC
They are deducted from net bank credit while computing ANBC
NABARD deposits count under agriculture, SIDBI under MSME and NHB under housing; all count towards the overall target and are added to net bank credit for ANBC
Only NABARD deposits count, and only towards the agriculture sub-target

solution.explanation: Outstanding deposits with NABARD on account of PSL shortfall count towards the agriculture sub-target; those with SIDBI and MUDRA under MSME lending; those with NHB under housing. All count for the overall PSL target and are added to net bank credit (NBC) in computing ANBC.
steps: All → overall target; added to NBC
solution.why_others_wrong: They do count towards sub-targets, are added to (not deducted from) NBC, and are not limited to NABARD.
solution.final_answer: Option C: NABARD deposits count under agriculture, SIDBI under MSME and NHB under housing; all count towards the overall target and are added to net bank credit for ANBC

fact_checks.claim: Outstanding deposits with NABARD on account of PSL shortfall are eligible to be reckoned towards Agriculture sub-target and overall PSL target; deposits with SIDBI and MUDRA under MSME lending; deposits with NHB under Housing; all outstanding deposits shall be added to Net Bank Credit for the computation of ANBC

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Bank loans for 'Agriculture Infrastructure' and for 'Food and Agro-processing' qualify as priority sector subject to an aggregate sanctioned limit per borrower from the banking system. What is that limit, and what happens if a borrower's aggregate exposure across banks exceeds it?

options.text: ₹100 crore; the entire exposure ceases to be priority sector
₹100 crore; only the excess over ₹100 crore loses PSL status
₹50 crore; the entire exposure ceases to be priority sector
₹50 crore; only the excess over ₹50 crore loses PSL status

solution.concept: Credit caps in agriculture PSL categories

steps: Limit: ₹100 crore per borrower across banks
Breach → whole exposure loses PSL status
solution.why_others_wrong: The limit is ₹100 crore, not ₹50 crore, and the whole exposure (not just the excess) is affected.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ₹100 crore; the entire exposure ceases to be priority sector

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A farmer takes a crop loan from a bank against the pledge of gold jewellery. The loan is sanctioned on the basis of the scale of finance for the crop. Can it be classified under priority sector (agriculture)?

Yes; PSL is activity- and beneficiary-specific, so gold collateral alone does not make it ineligible
Yes, but only if the loan is below ₹2 lakh
No, unless the farmer also mortgages agricultural land

solution.concept: PSL is based on activity, not collateral

The bank should have assessed the credit requirement (scale of finance) for the activity.
steps: Test the purpose and borrower, not the collateral
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no blanket bar on gold-backed loans; ₹2 lakh is the limit for waiving collateral, not an eligibility cap; a land mortgage is not required.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Yes; PSL is activity- and beneficiary-specific, so gold collateral alone does not make it ineligible

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

options.text: Yes, since the partner holds less than 2 hectares
Yes, but only for the partner's share of the loan
Yes, if the firm also qualifies as a micro enterprise
No; loans to partnership firms are not eligible for the SMF category on the basis of a partner's land holding

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

₹20,800 crore
₹21,800 crore

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

A customer's grievance against the bank's managing director personally

Maintainable only if the freeze lasted more than 30 days
To be transferred by the Ombudsman to the police for decision

The merchant accepting the payment

The National Informatics Centre

Only by visiting an RBI regional office with KYC documents

III. Where the DLG provider is itself a regulated entity, it must deduct the full outstanding DLG amount from its capital.
Which of the above is/are correct?

II and III only
I and III only
I only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: UPI handled 25.47 billion transactions worth ₹31.53 lakh crore in October 2026, against 24.07 billion worth ₹29.37 lakh crore in September 2026. The average daily value rose from ₹97,913 crore to ₹1,01,707 crore. Why did the average daily value rise by only about 3.9% when the monthly value rose by about 7.4%?

options.text: The number of transactions fell in October, which held down the daily average
Daily averages count only working days, and October had more holidays
October has 31 days against September's 30, so part of the monthly rise comes from the extra day
The monthly value includes UPI Lite payments, which the daily average excludes

solution.explanation: Monthly value rose 7.4% (29.37 → 31.53). Daily averages are monthly value ÷ days: 31.53 lakh crore ÷ 31 ≈ ₹1,01,700 crore and 29.37 lakh crore ÷ 30 ≈ ₹97,900 crore, a rise of about 3.9%. The gap is the day-count effect: 1.039 × 31/30 ≈ 1.074.
steps: 1.039 × (31 ÷ 30) ≈ 1.074 → the difference is the extra day
solution.shortcut: Growth in totals ≈ growth in daily average + growth in number of days (3.9% + 3.3% ≈ 7.4%).
solution.why_others_wrong: Volume rose (24.07 → 25.47 billion); the daily figures match value ÷ calendar days, so no working-day or UPI Lite adjustment is involved.
solution.final_answer: Option C: October has 31 days against September's 30, so part of the monthly rise comes from the extra day

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Atal Pension Yojana, what happens if the accumulated corpus earns lower returns than estimated and cannot support the guaranteed minimum pension?

options.text: The Central Government funds the shortfall; if returns are higher, the subscriber gets enhanced pension
The pension is cut in proportion to the shortfall
The bank holding the account must make good the shortfall
The subscriber must pay extra contributions to restore the corpus

solution.explanation: APY pays a fixed minimum pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 a month from 60. The minimum pension is guaranteed by the Government: any inadequacy from lower returns is funded by the Central Government, while higher returns give enhanced pension.
steps: Lower returns → Government funds the gap
solution.why_others_wrong: The pension is not cut, banks bear no liability, and no extra contribution is demanded.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Central Government funds the shortfall; if returns are higher, the subscriber gets enhanced pension

fact_checks.claim: If the accumulated corpus earns a lower than estimated return on investment and is inadequate to provide the minimum guaranteed pension, the Central Government would fund such inadequacy. Alternatively, if the returns on investment are higher, the subscribers would get enhanced pensionary benefits

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Up to what age can a PMJJBY member keep the life cover by renewing it, and what does the scheme pay on surrender or maturity?

options.text: Up to 70 years; return of premiums at maturity
Up to 50 years; a surrender value after five years
Up to 55 years; nothing, as it is pure term cover
Up to 60 years; a maturity bonus

solution.explanation: Entry into PMJJBY is allowed only up to 50, but cover ends at 55 (age nearest birthday), subject to annual renewal. It is a pure term policy with no investment component, so there is no maturity benefit or surrender value; only the nominee gets ₹2 lakh on death.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 is PMSBY's exit age; 50 is the entry limit; PMJJBY has no maturity, bonus or surrender benefit.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Up to 55 years; nothing, as it is pure term cover

fact_checks.claim: On attaining age 55 years (age near birth day), subject to annual renewal up to that date (entry, however, will not be possible beyond the age of 50 years)
PMJJBY is a pure term insurance policy, which covers only mortality with no investment component

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0, approved on 5 May 2026, what guarantee cover is provided on loans to eligible MSMEs and to eligible non-MSMEs?

options.text: 100% for MSMEs and 90% for non-MSMEs, with no guarantee fee
90% for MSMEs and 75% for non-MSMEs, at 1% fee
100% for both, with a fee of 0.5% a year
75% for MSMEs and 50% for non-MSMEs

solution.explanation: ECLGS 5.0, run by NCGTC for businesses hit by external disruptions, gives 100% guarantee on additional working capital to eligible MSMEs and 90% to eligible non-MSMEs (and 90% for scheduled passenger airlines), with no guarantee fee payable by lenders. It runs till 31 March 2027 or ₹2.55 lakh crore of guarantees.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other percentages and fees do not match the scheme.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 100% for MSMEs and 90% for non-MSMEs, with no guarantee fee

fact_checks.claim: Credit guarantee coverage: 100% guarantee for loans extended to eligible MSMEs and 90% guarantee coverage for eligible non-MSMEs; no guarantee fee is payable by MLIs under the scheme
The Government approved the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0 on 5th May 2026

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under CGTMSE's Credit Guarantee Scheme for banks, what is the standard annual guarantee fee (AGF) for guaranteed credit of up to ₹10 lakh?

options.text: 0.55% per annum
1.00% per annum
0.75% per annum
0.37% per annum

solution.explanation: Following CGTMSE's fee cuts (Circular 221, effective 1 April 2023), the standard AGF is 0.37% a year for the 0–10 lakh slab, 0.55% for above ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh and 0.60% for above ₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore. AGF is charged on the guaranteed amount in the first year and on the outstanding amount thereafter.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.55% is the next slab; 1.00% and 0.75% are not the rate for the smallest slab.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 0.37% per annum

fact_checks.claim: Slab 0-10 lakh: Revised Standard Rate 0.37 (pa); Above 10-50 lakh: 0.55; applicable to all guarantees approved/renewed on or after April 01, 2023

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under ECLGS 5.0, firm X (an MSME) had peak fund-based working capital outstanding of ₹45 crore in Q4 of FY 2025-26, and firm Y (an eligible non-MSME) had ₹800 crore. Both meet all other conditions. What maximum additional credit can each get, and with what guarantee cover?

options.text: X: ₹9 crore with 100% cover; Y: ₹160 crore with 90% cover
X: ₹9 crore with 100% cover; Y: ₹100 crore with 90% cover
X: ₹9 crore with 90% cover; Y: ₹100 crore with 100% cover
X: ₹45 crore with 100% cover; Y: ₹100 crore with 90% cover

solution.explanation: Additional credit is up to 20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding in Q4 FY26, capped at ₹100 crore per borrower. X: 20% × 45 = ₹9 crore, 100% guaranteed (MSME). Y: 20% × 800 = ₹160 crore, capped at ₹100 crore, 90% guaranteed (non-MSME).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹160 crore ignores the cap; the cover percentages are swapped in the third option; ₹45 crore ignores the 20% limit.
solution.final_answer: Option B: X: ₹9 crore with 100% cover; Y: ₹100 crore with 90% cover

fact_checks.claim: The scheme provides additional credit of up to 20% of the peak fund-based working capital outstanding during the fourth quarter of FY 2025-26, subject to a ceiling of ₹100 crore per borrower
100% guarantee for loans extended to eligible MSMEs and 90% guarantee coverage for eligible non-MSMEs

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Two CGTMSE-guaranteed loans of ₹30 lakh each turn NPA with ₹20 lakh in default. P is a micro enterprise of a woman entrepreneur in a district identified by RBI as credit deficient (ICDD); Q is a small enterprise of a borrower in the 'all other' category, outside any ICDD. What is the maximum guarantee cover on each?

solution.explanation: Women entrepreneurs get 90% cover, and MSEs in RBI's Identified Credit Deficient Districts get an extra 5 percentage points, so P gets 95%: 0.95 × 20 = ₹19 lakh. 'All other' borrowers get 75%: 0.75 × 20 = ₹15 lakh.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹18 lakh ignores the ICDD addition; 80% for Q would need an ICDD location; 85% applies to other categories.
solution.final_answer: Option C: P: ₹19 lakh (95%); Q: ₹15 lakh (75%)

fact_checks.claim: Women entrepreneurs / MSE promoted by Agniveers 90%; All other category of borrowers 75%; the extent of guarantee coverage for MSEs situated in Identified Credit Deficient Districts (ICDD) by RBI is additional 5% over and above the applicable guarantee coverage (for 90% it would be 95%)
